reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it presents Gigamax as a “100% legit” arbitrage bot and directs viewers to register and make a stated USDT deposit. It shows a crypto-arbitrage participation flow requesting personal, account, referral, and USDT-address information, along with deposit confirmation controls and withdrawal examples. The material does not establish that any deposits, withdrawals, profits, or credential use were completed or genuine.

citations.quote: Arbitrage | Gigamax real Arbitrage bot 100% legit
If you want to register, you can deposit $50

opening.argument: The material does not establish a guaranteed return or completed investment outcome. Its language is conditional and operational: it describes arbitrage options, minimum deposits, and platform functions, while the screen presents selectable USDT products rather than proof of earnings. The title’s “100% legit” is a general characterization, not evidence that viewers will profit. At most, this is an invitation to evaluate a trading service whose actual performance remains unverified.

citations.quote: Arbitrage | Gigamax real Arbitrage bot 100% legit
The $200 is what this trade has in it's maximum
Arbitration only happens when the currency itself is in a good situation

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening treats a title and interface controls as proof of deception, but they establish only that arbitrage products and a registration flow are being presented. The quoted deposit instruction does not itself promise a return, and the frames do not prove that money was accepted, that credentials were misused, or that any displayed activity was fabricated. Lack of proof of performance is not proof of a scam.

citations.quote: If you want to register, you can deposit $50

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The presentation goes beyond neutral risk discussion: it labels the bot “100% legit,” directs viewers to register, and identifies deposit amounts and USDT trading products. The interface shows fields for passwords, a USDT address, and a referral ID, while the platform presents withdrawal examples. Those features make the promotional framing materially stronger than the claim that this is merely unverified commentary.

citations.quote: Arbitrage | Gigamax real Arbitrage bot 100% legit

opening.argument: The video's observable structure is a walkthrough of how the platform works. It explains registration, account fields, arbitrage selections, deposit limits, and transaction steps, while the frames show the dashboard, market-price screen, product choices, and confirmation controls. That is consistent with an operational demonstration of a technology platform, not evidence that the presenter completed a transaction or guaranteed an outcome. The garbled narration also cannot reliably support stronger claims about what the presenter intended.

citations.quote: Now it has been sent and you can view your new email by tapping on the button

rebuttal.rebuttal: The reference interpretation assumes that showing a workflow is solicitation, but a tutorial necessarily demonstrates the same screens a user would encounter. The cited title is promotional wording, yet it does not show that the presenter verified a deposit or obtained a return. A visible registration flow can explain software operation without establishing that the service is fraudulent.

citations.quote: In this case, you can register here

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Calling the video a tutorial does not remove its practical solicitation. The narration repeatedly tells viewers to register, deposit, and contact the site administrator, while the screens show the exact account and trading paths. A demonstration can still promote a financial service; the absence of a completed transaction does not undermine the observable instructions to participate.

If you have any questions, please do not hesitate to contact me via the admin of the website

opening.argument: The evidence is also compatible with ordinary promotion of a software-based trading service. The platform displays different arbitrage products, stated minimum and maximum deposit fields, market-price information, and account-management screens. Crucially, the supplied material does not show a guaranteed-return promise, a completed withdrawal, a downline-income scheme, or proof that credentials were actually collected or used. A referral field and a deposit control may be ordinary platform features; they do not, by themselves, establish a scam mechanism.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The reference side combines separate facts into a mechanism that the evidence does not complete. A registration form is not proof of credential misuse, a deposit amount is not proof that funds were taken, and a product screen is not proof of a false return. Even the opening concedes that completed deposits, withdrawals, profits, and credential use are not established; that concession leaves ordinary service promotion as a plausible reading.

citations.quote: If you want to register, you can deposit $50

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The missing-completion point does not make the content ordinary commerce. The video combines a “100% legit” claim with instructions to register and deposit, USDT-address and password fields, arbitrage products, and displayed withdrawal activity. The evidence need not prove a completed theft to show promotion of the very funding flow associated with the alleged service; the interface itself supplies the relevant mechanism.
